terms.name: LoCo
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report math and code experiments. These results have not been independently reproduced by this app.
terms.meaning: LoCo trains a reasoning model to decide whether to continue reasoning or conclude from its current state.

how.title: Find likely overthinking
how.detail: Locate reasoning states where a shorter continuation might already reach a correct answer.

how.title: Create a local comparison
how.detail: Freeze each prefix and generate shorter, verified continuations from that same state.

how.title: Train the stopping decision
how.detail: Use DPO on state-conditioned preference pairs, teaching when to stop rather than imposing one length target on every problem.

terms.why: Reasoning length affects response time and serving cost. Efficiency matters only if the model preserves correctness on your actual tasks.
terms.example: A math assistant could learn to stop after a sufficient derivation instead of adding redundant checks. The method requires training access and verified examples.
terms.experiment: Inspect the accuracy–length tradeoff on ten verifiable problems before attempting to train a stopping policy.
terms.caution: The paper studies particular math and code benchmarks. The POC explores stopping decisions and does not reproduce LoCo’s DPO training.

source.title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression

poc.goal: Find where shorter reasoning stops being sufficient on ten problems.
requirements: Ten math or code problems with independently checked answers
An open reasoning model exposing generated traces, or public examples from the paper
A spreadsheet for correctness, output length and elapsed time
steps: Collect a complete trace and answer for each problem, using fixed prompts and sampling settings.
Choose two plausible stopping points in each trace. Ask the same model to finish from each prefix.
Check every answer against the independent answer or executable tests. Record length and time.
Compare shorter correct continuations with the baseline and inspect every failure.
successCriteria: Every claimed improvement retains a verified correct final answer.
Report length and correctness together for all ten problems, including failures.
poc.limitations: This is a diagnostic exercise, without preference-pair training. It cannot establish the paper’s reported model improvements.

terms.name: ToolSpace
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report replay-verified environments and benchmark experiments. Transfer beyond those environments remains to be established.
terms.meaning: ToolSpace builds agent training and evaluation environments from dependencies observed between real tool calls, then turns replayable sequences into tasks.

how.title: Build a tool graph
how.detail: Extract data, state and retry dependencies from adjacent tool calls in execution traces.

how.title: Construct environments
how.detail: Cluster connected tools. Synthesize databases for state-mutating tools and replay recorded returns for query or stateless tools.

how.title: Verify generated tasks
how.detail: Use state-aware walks and rollback, translate successful chains into tasks, and keep those whose outcome assertions replay from the starting state.

terms.why: Your tool traces can help reveal workflow failures that isolated tool-call tests miss. Repeatable state and executable checks are central to a useful evaluation.
terms.example: A mock support task could retrieve a customer, update a ticket and verify the final ticket state. Every replay starts from a clean snapshot.
terms.experiment: Build five replayable evaluation tasks from tool traces in a mock support workspace.
terms.caution: Trace-derived environments inherit the coverage and biases of the traces. This small POC illustrates the idea and does not reproduce the full synthesis or training pipeline.

source.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents

poc.goal: Create five tasks with clean starting states and repeatable outcome checks.
requirements: A mock ticket database or JSON file with no production data
Five successful traces with tool names, arguments and returns
A script to reset state and replay calls
steps: Record five workflows against the mock workspace, including reads and state changes.
Connect calls where a returned value becomes a later argument, and record separate state dependencies.
Write initial snapshots and final assertions, then describe each task without revealing the tool sequence.
Replay every task twice from clean state, then compare an agent’s final assertions with the baseline.
successCriteria: Every retained task produces identical outcome assertions on two clean replays.
Report agent task success separately from environment replay reliability.
poc.limitations: Five inspected traces cannot establish the full method’s environment coverage, benchmark difficulty, or training benefits.

terms.name: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning
terms.meaning: A research approach that trains a speculative draft model to disagree at important reasoning points, causing target verification to restart there. It uses rejection timing to manage numerical precision during long agent tasks.

how.title: Find sensitive decision points
how.detail: The authors examine where numerical differences within speculative verification windows can affect later agent decisions.

how.title: Train for selective disagreement
how.detail: Their draft model learns adversarial preferences around these points, seeking useful rejections rather than maximizing acceptance everywhere.

how.title: Restart target verification
how.detail: Draft disagreement restarts verification at selected points. The authors report coding benchmark gains under their evaluated settings.

terms.why: For a PM, decoding speed and task success can interact. Evaluate an acceleration method on completed tasks as well as tokens per second.
terms.example: A coding-agent evaluation could compare task pass rates and runtime across speculative-decoding configurations, rather than choosing the highest draft acceptance rate alone.
terms.experiment: Use a small rounding simulation to explore why numerical settings can affect repeated decisions. This is a diagnostic exercise, not an ASR reproduction.
terms.caution: The evidence comes from the authors’ long-horizon coding experiments. Results on other tasks and runtimes remain uncertain. Reproducing ASR requires model and inference-engine work beyond this exercise.

source.title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents

terms.evidenceNote: The authors report coding experiments with trained draft models. This app has not reproduced those results.

poc.goal: See how rounding and restart intervals can change a chain of toy decisions.
requirements: A spreadsheet or Python with its standard library
A table with columns for step, reference value, rounded value, decision and mismatch
steps: Create 40 rows. Start two values at 0.4. At each row compute next = 3.9 × value × (1 − value). Keep one column at full precision; round the other to three decimal places after each update.
Record a toy decision at every row: A if the value is at least 0.5, B otherwise. Count disagreements between the two columns.
Repeat with restart windows of 4, 8 and 16 rows. At each boundary copy the current reference value into the rounded column, then continue updating.
Repeat all settings from starting values 0.2 and 0.7. Keep every result, including settings where restarting does not reduce disagreement.
successCriteria: Record the first disagreement and total mismatched decisions across all 40 rows for each of the three starting values.
Produce a comparison table for the three restart windows and the no-restart baseline; account for every trial without claiming an agent accuracy gain.
poc.limitations: This toy recurrence illustrates numerical sensitivity and resets. It contains no draft model, target model, learned rejection policy or real agent task, so it cannot test ASR performance.

terms.generatedBy: AI-written · source and POC checked · suggested exercise

terms.name: In-context learning
terms.meaning: In-context learning lets a pretrained model infer a task from demonstrations in its prompt, without changing its weights. A recent circuit study examines how a label memory, class-matching attention and a repetition signal support this behavior in a controlled sentence-classification setting.

how.title: Store the demonstrated labels
how.detail: In the studied models, each label position carries the label identity in its residual stream. Middle-layer heads write the preceding demonstration’s class as a key at that position.

how.title: Match the query class
how.detail: Upper-layer heads match the query’s class against those stored keys and copy the corresponding label values.

how.title: Enable the readout
how.detail: An early signal indicates that a label has repeated. Without that signal, readers attend to the prompt’s start and no label is favored.

how.title: Keep a separate recency effect
how.detail: Other heads suppress the most recently seen label. The paper treats this as a separate component, rather than the repetition gate.

terms.why: This gives builders a specific hypothesis for prompt experiments: demonstrations can supply a temporary label mapping. Test example choice and label assignments on your own tasks before assuming that more context will help.
terms.example: Demonstrations can map the classes cat and dog to arbitrary labels such as dax and wug. A new query’s class can then retrieve the demonstrated label mapping during the forward pass.
terms.experiment: Explore a simplified label memory and repetition gate with six hand-written query cases.
terms.caution: The circuit evidence comes from controlled classification experiments in three small transformers, with additional tests within one model family. The toy below does not establish how other models or production tasks behave.
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report activation patching, head ablations and steering experiments. This app has not reproduced their neural-circuit results.

poc.goal: Explore a simplified label memory and repetition gate with six hand-written query cases.
requirements: Python 3 with its standard library, or a spreadsheet
Three label sets: A = dax,wug,dax; B = dax,wug,zop; C = wug,dax,wug
steps: For each label set, run two queries: (1,0) and (0,1). Calculate the dot product of the query and each of the three class-key vectors. These are hand-chosen class features, not model activations.

Build an ungated baseline: sum the matching scores for each label, then divide by the total score to make a label distribution. For A, the first query gives dax a total score of 2 and wug a score of 0.

Add the repetition gate: if any label repeats in the demonstration set, retain the baseline distribution. If every label is unique, return an equal distribution over the unique labels instead. This models the source’s presence-versus-absence condition in a simplified way.
Compare A with B to inspect the gate, then A with C to inspect relabeling. Keep the class keys and queries fixed. Record all six outputs and their ungated baselines.
successCriteria: Across the four repeated-label query cases in A and C, the highest-scoring labels follow each set’s demonstrated mapping. Relabeling A to C changes both query predictions without changing the class keys.
For both all-unique cases in B, the gated version returns 1/3 for each of its three labels, while the ungated baseline is nonuniform. Omitting the gate must therefore fail this check.
poc.limitations: This hand-written lookup illustrates selected components. It uses no neural weights or attention heads, omits the separate recency-suppression effect, and cannot reproduce the paper’s causal interventions or measure a real model’s ICL performance.

items.releaseNotes:
## New Features

- The opt-in terminal workspace supports multiple side-chat tabs. Switch between them with the keyboard or mouse, and reopen saved local side chats after restarting Codex. (#59784, #60152, #60181)
- Search older tasks from the agent command center by name, prompt preview, or working directory. (#60286)
- Turn on **Collapse turn details** in the full-screen transcript to fold completed activity beneath each prompt while keeping answers visible and tool output searchable. (#60554, #60555, #60556, #60557)
- Add or edit custom model providers from the terminal. With custom gateway onboarding enabled, you can create a provider during sign-in and use a device code for supported gateways over SSH or without a local browser. (#59779, #60009, #60186, #60486, #60662)
- Press `Ctrl+S` in the terminal report editor to save a diagnostic ZIP locally, even when uploads are disabled. (#60542)
- With the opt-in Cloud connection on macOS and Linux, send images, choose a model and reasoning effort, and archive or restore Cloud conversations from the terminal. (#59828, #60061, #60635, #60651)

## Bug Fixes

- `codex exec` keeps project configuration and MCP servers disabled in untrusted directories, even with `--sandbox workspace-write`. Use `--trust` with `codex exec` or `codex review` to explicitly save project trust. (#60041)
- **Yes, clear context and implement** now hands the full approved plan to the fresh session and keeps the current session open if the handoff fails. (#60763)
- Fixed Windows sandbox handling for quoted `cmd.exe` paths and for PowerShell sessions whose working directory has an unreadable parent. (#60624, #60647)
- Pasted images on macOS retain their intended orientation and use native PNG or JPEG clipboard data when available. (#60455)
- The terminal no longer stays busy waiting for MCP servers that a shared app server did not report. (#60280, #60622)
- Interrupted turns now close cleanly, and delayed aborts or file approval cancellations no longer interrupt a later turn. (#59910, #60700)

## Documentation

- Updated the `openai-docs` skill to focus on Codex and ChatGPT Work questions and first-time API setup, with dedicated guidance for configuring Codex across a team. (#59944, #59949)
- Documented how app-server clients can list models or authorize a gateway for a configured provider without changing the default provider. (#59776, #59819)

## Chores

- Updated bundled SQLite to 3.54 to pick up write-ahead log fixes. (#60432)
- Plugin marketplace upgrades can reuse Git objects already on disk, reducing repeat downloads. (#60528)

items.releaseNotes:
## New Features

- Browse model providers under Sessions → Model providers and choose the default for new chats. (#59541, #59722)
- Enable `features.tui_workspace` to view a side conversation beside the main chat. Drag the divider to resize the panes or press `leader z` to zoom the focused pane. (#58992, #59527, #59595)
- Attach recordings when using an audio-capable model. Codex skips confirmed rejected recordings on later turns and uses clip duration to keep more short recordings in context. (#59234, #59268)
- Enable `features.image_generation_animation` to generate or edit animated GIFs with optional frame count and timing controls. (#59073)
- Fullscreen Codex displays image previews and pets in tmux on Ghostty and Kitty with `allow-passthrough all`. (#59579, #59580)
- Set `tui.notification_method = "osc777"` for terminal notifications. Approval notifications show longer command previews and distinguish terminal input from network access requests. (#59256)

## Bug Fixes

- Local TUI history and resume pickers filter newly created threads by the signed-in ChatGPT account. (#58918)
- Open and resumed chats use their saved model provider after you change the default for new chats. (#59503)
- The TUI renders replies interrupted by tool calls as a single Markdown message and restores reasoning summaries when replaying a conversation. (#59698, #59700)
- Steering messages reach running turns when sent during the final transcript save or after switching back to a long-running chat. (#58877, #58998)
- Fuzzy file search gives filename matches more weight so matching parent directories are less likely to crowd them out. (#59709)
- Idle local MCP servers on Windows leave filesystem I/O available to the rest of Codex. (#59726)

## Documentation

- The app-server reference covers listing model providers, creating custom gateways, and updating gateway, Bedrock, and GCP settings. (#58845, #58876)

## Chores

- Codex warns when `features.multi_agent` is explicitly configured and points to `agents.enabled` for disabling subagent tools. (#59479)
- Contributors can run Bazel CI jobs locally without BuildBuddy credentials. (#59055)

items.releaseNotes:
## What's changed

- Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
- Added `engines["claude-code"]` to `plugin.json`: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
- Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to `claude plugin validate`; each finding is a warning, and `--strict` fails on it
- Added to `claude plugin validate` the `$` nouns a mod's `engine.create` hook adds, withholds or replaces
- Added support for `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL` in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
- Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
- Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in `claude -p` and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
- Added `.docx` support to Artifact tool asset uploads
- Added a `/diff to close` hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the `?` shortcut guide
- Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a `*` in a variable's value, such as `Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)`
- Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
- Added a one-time startup notice naming `CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE` when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES` (available since 2.1.318): set it to `1` to turn off subagent progress summaries and the requests that write them (anthropics/claude-code#86879)
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_HINT_COMMAND`, which a program that starts Claude Code can set to have the exit hint name its own resume command
- Added `unsetOptionCount` to the `claude plugin install --json` result: how many `userConfig` options are not yet set
- Added `isPromptCovered` to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt
- Fixed running `/compact` again, or after a command such as `/context`, summarizing away a message that Claude had not answered yet
- Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
- Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
- Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to `settings.json` moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
- Fixed `claude plugin` commands and `claude mcp list` signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed
- Fixed Edit and Bash running out of memory on certain `/proc` files, and Edit hanging or running out of memory on devices and named pipes
- Fixed Claude Code failing to start, or to clear stored credentials at sign-out, when saving its configuration file failed with "Out of memory"
- Fixed requests sent without streaming failing on errors that streamed requests recover from, such as a rejected image, thinking block or beta header
- Fixed `ExitWorktree`, the worktree exit dialog and `/resume` leaving the session in the wrong folder when the folder the shell was in before entering the worktree had been deleted
- Fixed accents and other combining marks sometimes landing left of the text, leaving stale copies on screen, or silently disappearing when text wraps
- Fixed the last key of a key chord, such as Enter in ctrl+x enter, acting on a dialog's text field when the chord's own action isn't available there
- Fixed `ps` processes piling up when the process listing Claude Code runs before stopping a command takes too long
- Fixed subagent transcripts and large tool results being saved apart from the session's transcript after entering a worktree created by a `WorktreeCreate` hook or belonging to a nested repository
- Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile moving to another sign-in when `/fork`, the Left arrow or `--bg` continued it in the background; reopen any session that was open during the update
- Fixed a background session sending a conversation under another sign-in when its named Anthropic profile is missing, changed or overridden; it now stops and says so
- Fixed a session on an API key, auth token or workload identity from its shell (not a setup token) moving to another sign-in in the background; it now stops and says so
- Fixed MCP tool calls ending in the sign-in server's error, such as `TOKEN_EXPIRED`, instead of asking you to sign in again
- Fixed an expired claude.ai login showing "Credit balance too low" when a saved Console key or `ant auth login` profile without credit was used instead
- Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile being handed to an older background service that could not keep its sign-in; it now says to restart the service
- Fixed a background session's sign-in leaving the previous account's login or other credentials in place; it now clears them for every session on the computer, and a refused sign-in can leave no login
- Fixed background sessions moving between a profile and the stored login when an update restarted them
- Fixed sessions opened before a sign-in keeping signed-out feature flags after the sign-in
- Fixed sessions that kept failing after a Claude apps gateway sign-in expired: once you sign in again with `/login` in another terminal, they carry on at the next message
- Fixed the billing notice naming your `ant auth login` organization when a custom `X-Api-Key` header is set
- macOS: Fixed "Not logged in · Please run /login" coming back right after a successful `/login` or a token refresh when the keychain was slow to answer
- Fixed turns failing in Claude Desktop when an organization's gateway answers an expired token with 403: Claude Code now asks Desktop for a fresh token and retries
- Fixed the error shown when Amazon Bedrock refuses your account a model: it no longer says to refresh your AWS credentials, it says to enable the model
- Fixed the `awsAuthRefresh` or `gcpAuthRefresh` command sometimes running twice for one request when three or more sessions needed a fresh sign-in at once
- Fixed the `claude -p` warning about an ended claude.ai login to say that `claude auth logout` also removes saved MCP server logins and plugin secrets
- Fixed Bash permission prompts offering "don't ask again" for commands that write to sensitive paths such as `.git` or `.claude`, where the saved rule did not stop the next prompt
- Fixed a case where some `lsof` commands ran without a permission prompt
- Fixed Bash commands that write a file with `cat > file <<EOF` being shown as "Read 1 file"
- Fixed a case where Bash permission checks judged an `rm` from the wrong folder and skipped the dangerous-removal prompt under bypass permissions or a Bash allow rule
- Fixed `--permission-mode auto` or a settings `defaultMode: auto` starting in a mode that could allow more when auto mode was unavailable. It now starts in Manual mode, which asks first
- Fixed plan files sometimes being written outside the project when `plansDirectory` is set; a write that can't be shown to stay inside the project is now refused
- Fixed a permission prompt when Claude read the output of its own background command or agent after entering a worktree
- Fixed a case where Bash permission checks missed part of a command
- Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox could switch off during a session
- Fixed Bash allow rules with an attached wildcard, such as `Bash(ls*)`, skipping the permission prompt in some cases; a rule that names a variable, such as `Bash(NODE_ENV*)`, now asks
- Fixed auto mode running behind a gateway at `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` on a model whose gateway name contains "haiku"; such a model, other than `claude-haiku-5-5`, is now refused, as Haiku 4.5 is
- Fixed Bash deny and ask rules missing some commands run through `sudo`, `env` and similar wrappers
- Fixed Bash allow rules written with combined `sudo` flags skipping the permission prompt in some cases
- Fixed `sandbox.excludedCommands` letting a command that it does not name run outside the sandbox in some cases
- Fixed a case where the Write and Edit tools could write to a path covered by a `Read` deny rule
- Fixed a case where a Bash command ran without a permission prompt for zsh users with certain non-default shell options set
- Fixed the Bash sandbox not fully protecting Claude Code's own config on installs still using the legacy config file
- Fixed a permission prompt from a mod's `tool.check` hook naming every plugin hooked on the tool instead of the one that asked
- Fixed sandboxed commands being able to read Claude Code's file checkpoint copies under the config directory
- Fixed a rewind sometimes changing your permission mode
- Fixed project settings sometimes being read through a symbolic link that leads to a different folder than the one Claude Code checked
- Fixed HTTP hooks failing with HTTP 500 on Linux when `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB` is set and `sandbox.enabled` is off
- Fixed `claude -p` and the Agent SDK running Bash unsandboxed when `--settings` or SDK settings that turn the sandbox on fail validation; Claude Code now stops at start-up and names the invalid setting
- Fixed `/export` silently stopping early after a long run of calls to an MCP tool that is no longer loaded

ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
items.summary: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry,…
items.abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

items.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
items.summary: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in…
items.abstract: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

items.title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
items.summary: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two…
items.abstract: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

items.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
items.summary: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown…
items.abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.

items.title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
items.summary: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network…
items.abstract: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.

items.title: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
items.summary: Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens…
items.abstract: Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task. Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.

items.title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
items.summary: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can…
items.abstract: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.

items.title: Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences
items.summary: Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This…
items.abstract: Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

items.title: Goal Encoding in LLMs
items.summary: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through…
items.abstract: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.

items.title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
items.summary: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native…
items.abstract: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.

items.title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings,…
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.

items.title: Synthesis Smuggling: Maliciously Hiding Inferred Personal Attributes in LLM Outputs
items.summary: We propose Synthesis Smuggling, a novel threat model in which an adversarial LLM infers sensitive information about a user from routine assistance-seeking interactions and steganographically…
items.abstract: We propose Synthesis Smuggling, a novel threat model in which an adversarial LLM infers sensitive information about a user from routine assistance-seeking interactions and steganographically encodes that into innocuous-looking model-generated content. The user may then unknowingly transmit that information by sharing the generated artifact, say as an email, social-media post, or message, through ordinary communication channels. An adversary monitoring these channels can discover this information. We demonstrate this threat by training two open-weight models to infer gender and age-group labels from conversational cues and encode their predictions using invisible characters or word choices. These results show that user-shared model outputs can become a covert channel for personal inferences, even when the model itself has no direct means of contacting an adversary.

items.title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
items.summary: We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic…
items.abstract: We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds.

items.title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
items.summary: Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand-crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. A natural assumption…
items.abstract: Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand-crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. A natural assumption is that more powerful and more expensive models consistently yield better heuristics. We challenge this empirically: across multiple NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, we find no consistent advantage for larger, costlier models. This raises a deeper question: given a pool of LLMs spanning frontier and freely hosted or open-weight models, how should one adaptively select which model to invoke at each step of the search? The challenge is non-trivial. The optimal LLM may shift over the course of a run, and because one LLM's output seeds the context for subsequent calls, each model's reward signal is non-stationary and entangled across the heuristic population, thus violating the independence assumptions of classical online decision-making settings. We address this through Ballad (Bandit-based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery), an online bandit algorithm that learns to orchestrate a pool of LLMs into an ensemble that matches or exceeds what any soloist LLM achieves alone. This orchestration is powered by an LLM selection policy that favors rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages, a DAG-based credit propagation mechanism through the genealogy of the heuristic population, and discounting of stale observations to remain attuned to each model's current utility. Across five NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems and a pool of four models of varying capability and cost, Ballad not only matches the best individual LLM in hindsight but, in several cases, surpasses every individual model while reducing API cost by up to 65.6% relative to always using the strongest model.

items.title: When Both Sides Adapt: The Challenges of Evaluating Interactive LLM Systems
items.summary: In interactive systems where users engage with LLMs, users are adaptive and, after observing LLM responses, can change their prompting strategy, as well as the…
items.abstract: In interactive systems where users engage with LLMs, users are adaptive and, after observing LLM responses, can change their prompting strategy, as well as the type and difficulty of subsequent tasks. Thus model responses can influence the set of prompts on which the model is subsequently evaluated. We study the implications of this user adaptivity and prompt endogeneity for the evaluation of LLMs. We define two classes of estimands for comparing models: the common-distribution effect, which compares model performance on the same distribution of prompts, and the induced-distribution effect, which compares each model on the prompt distribution generated through user interaction. We show that offline benchmark evaluation and live A/B testing target different quantities, with the standard difference-in-means estimators for the two methods converging to the common-distribution effect and the induced-distribution effect, respectively. This distinction can affect decision-making: the two comparisons can rank models differently and lead to discrepancies in deployment recommendations. We characterize when such ranking reversals occur and provide a sufficient condition under which the rankings are guaranteed to agree. This result provides a practical heuristic for assessing whether offline evaluation is sufficient to reproduce the decision suggested by a live experiment. Third, we show, in a stylized linear model of interactions, that user adaptivity can increase variance in estimation. Finally, we discuss implications of user adaptivity for the interpretation of experiments and show that adaptivity creates a common mechanism leading to common evaluation challenges, such as reward hacking and novelty effects. Together, this work highlights the necessity of measuring both model performance as well as changes in the user behavior that the model induces.

items.title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
items.summary: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al…
items.abstract: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts

items.title: Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
items.summary: Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions…
items.abstract: Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions to resolve ambiguous answers. But oral exams scale poorly. In this paper, we present scalable conversational assessment, an LLM-based system that conducts interactive text-based conversations with students to assess their ability to make and support an argument. We use a two-agent architecture to separate concerns and reduce the likelihood that answers are leaked to the student: the interviewer interacts directly with the student, but only receives guidance about the next question to ask the student; the hidden evaluator knows the goals of the whole activity, tracks the student's progress using a rubric, and guides the interviewer on when to follow-up on the current question or proceed to the next question. The system was first tested using a collection of simulated students with LLM personas of a particular ability level or adversarial tactic (e.g., answer-extractors, prompt-injectors, confident fabricators). A novel element of this evaluation was that it required the use of a fictional assessment topic to prevent personas that shouldn't have information from using knowledge present in the LLM's pre-training. The system was also deployed in a small, elective AI literacy course in both formative and summative contexts. Through manual and post-facto AI review of the transcripts we identified opportunities to improve the follow-up question generation and ensure that grading only credited ideas that the student (and not the interviewer) contributed.

items.title: Introducing Feedback Delays to Non-Delayed Adversarial MDPs: Optimal $\sqrt S$ and $\sqrt K$ Dependencies in Tabular and Linear AMDPs
items.summary: We study regret minimization in episodic Adversarial Markov Decision Processes (AMDPs) with unknown transitions and bandit feedback. In tabular AMDPs with $S$ states, $A$ actions,…
items.abstract: We study regret minimization in episodic Adversarial Markov Decision Processes (AMDPs) with unknown transitions and bandit feedback. In tabular AMDPs with $S$ states, $A$ actions, and horizon $H$, the best known $K$-episode regret is $\tilde O(HS\sqrt{AK})$, whose $\sqrt S$ gap to the $Ω(H\sqrt{SAK})$ lower bound has long remained open. In linear AMDPs with $d$-dimensional features, after a five-year line of improvements starting from $K^{14/15}$, computationally efficient algorithms without a simulator or exploratory assumptions still only attain $\tilde O(K^{3/4})$ regret. A common challenge in both settings is to estimate the Q-function of a changing policy: past data comes from earlier policies that differ from (and are correlated with) the current one, while freezing the policy for future episodes worsens the dependency on $K$. We instead propose a general technique called introduced feedback delays: we estimate the Q-function of the policy using future episodes while still updating the policy, as if the feedback were delayed. While feedback delays are usually an obstacle imposed by the environment, here they are introduced voluntarily and, perhaps surprisingly, come at no extra cost. We develop Geometric Resampling with Rejection (GRR) to account for policy changes during the delay, and threshold the visitation probabilities to avoid long delays on rarely visited state-action pairs. With this unified technique, our policy optimization algorithms achieve, with high probability, $\tilde O(\text{poly}(H)\sqrt{SAK})$ regret in tabular AMDPs, resolving the open problem; and $\tilde O(\text{poly}(d,H)\sqrt K)$ regret in linear AMDPs, giving the first efficient algorithm optimal in $K$. They also naturally extend to delayed AMDPs with a total feedback delay $\mathfrak D$, yielding the first bounds optimal in $S$ and $\mathfrak D$ (tabular) and in $K$ and $\mathfrak D$ (linear).

items.title: MALNISI-Infused Graph Construction and Weighted Contrastive Loss based GAT for Unsupervised Representation Learning in HSI
items.summary: Hyperspectral images (HSI) possess discriminating spectral characteristics with respect to land utilization due to high-dimensional information. Recently, unsupervised representation learning using graph neural networks has…
items.abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) possess discriminating spectral characteristics with respect to land utilization due to high-dimensional information. Recently, unsupervised representation learning using graph neural networks has unveiled these utilization-specific complex spectral relations. This article has three main contributions. First, it proposes an index, the Mean Absolute Local Neighborhood Inverse Spectral Index (MALNISI), which measures the similarity between two pixels based on their neighborhood information. The index is used to construct a weighted adjacency matrix, giving the HSI a graph structure. Second, it proposes an upgraded Graph Attention Network that learns compact latent representations of hyperspectral data from the constructed graph. In this network, an enhanced multi-head attention mechanism incorporates the MALNISI weights as an auxiliary feature to emphasize learned attention between neighboring pixels. To alleviate over-smoothing and preserve fine-grained spectral details, the architecture integrates residual connections, skip projections, and feature normalization, which together enhance representation capability, stabilize learning, and accelerate convergence. Third, it proposes a weighted contrastive loss function that incorporates neighborhood-aware MALNISI between connected pixels, encouraging strongly connected pixels in the high-dimensional space to remain close in the latent space, and weakly connected pixels to stay apart. The resulting discriminative low-dimensional embeddings are then clustered using spectral clustering. Experimental analysis on six benchmark HSI datasets demonstrates the efficiency and necessity of the three aforementioned contributions, and the comparative study highlights superior performance over fourteen state-of-the-art approaches.

items.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
items.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable…
items.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $λ=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most $0.02$ in all but one model-rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning-forgetting frontier. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomohiro-sawada/lora-capacity-utilization

items.title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
items.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and…
items.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.

items.title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
items.summary: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free…
items.abstract: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

items.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose…
items.abstract: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

items.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance…
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models
items.summary: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them…
items.abstract: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.

items.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
items.summary: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a…
items.abstract: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

items.title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI
items.summary: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions…
items.abstract: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

items.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
items.summary: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent…
items.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

items.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
items.summary: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin…
items.abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

items.title: Disentangling Spurious Correlations: How IRM Handles Diverse Shortcuts in Text Classification
items.summary: In NLP, models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often exploit spurious correlations, such as dialectal markers, at the expense of robust linguistic features, thereby…
items.abstract: In NLP, models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often exploit spurious correlations, such as dialectal markers, at the expense of robust linguistic features, thereby degrading their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) aims to suppress such shortcuts by identifying predictive relationships that remain stable across environments, but its practical utility for NLP remains debated. We use a causality-driven framework to evaluate IRM under three shortcut-generating mechanisms: label-generated features, confounding, and selection bias. Our results show that IRM successfully rejects shortcuts across the evaluated causal and anti-causal structures, including under limited environmental variation and increasing label noise. We then extend our analysis beyond controlled synthetic artifacts to two less constrained settings: gender-profession associations in Bias in Bios and semantically loaded actor-name shortcuts in ActorCorr. These experiments show that invariant learning can mitigate more realistic textual shortcuts, while semantically meaningful features require careful calibration of the invariance penalty.
